## Learning goals

- Write a GMM as $p(z)\,p(x\mid z)$ (dice then Gaussian).
- Run the E-step: responsibilities via Bayes.
- Set up the M-step objective for $(\alpha_j,\mu_j,\Sigma_j)$.
- See why a fitted GMM is also a **generative** sampler.

---

## Before this clicks

A **Gaussian mixture model (GMM)** with $M$ components:

$$
p_\theta(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} \alpha_j\,\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_j,\Sigma_j),\qquad \alpha_j\ge 0,\;\sum_j\alpha_j=1.
$$

Direct MLE hits $\log\sum_j(\cdots)$ — hard. Introduce a discrete latent $Z\in\{1,\ldots,M\}$ and use EM.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Latent-variable story

$$
p_\theta(x,z) = p_\theta(z)\,p_\theta(x\mid z).
$$

- $Z\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_M)$ (roll an $M$-faced die).
- $X\mid Z=j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_j,\Sigma_j)$.

Marginalizing $Z$ recovers the mixture. Parameters:

$$
\theta = \{\alpha_j,\mu_j,\Sigma_j\}_{j=1}^{M}.
$$

### 2. E-step (responsibilities)

With current $\theta^{(t)}$,

$$
q^{(t+1)}(Z=j\mid x) = p_{\theta^{(t)}}(Z=j\mid x)
= \frac{\alpha_j^{(t)}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_j^{(t)},\Sigma_j^{(t)})}{\sum_{k=1}^{M}\alpha_k^{(t)}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})}.
$$

This is a discrete distribution over $j$ for each data point (do it for every $x_i$).

### 3. M-step setup

Form

$$
F(\theta,q^{(t+1)}) = \mathbb{E}_{q^{(t+1)}}\!\left[\log\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q^{(t+1)}(z)}\right]
$$

and maximize in $\theta$. For one point, the useful part is

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{M} q(Z=j\mid x)\Bigl[\log\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)+\log\alpha_j\Bigr],
$$

then sum over $i=1,\ldots,n$. Closed forms (derived in Tutorial 8): weighted means, weighted covariances, and $\alpha_j$ = average responsibility.

### 4. GMM as a generative model

After fitting: sample $j\sim\alpha$, then sample $x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_j,\Sigma_j)$. If the mixture matched the data distribution well (KL / likelihood), samples look like data. Course context: use GMMs to estimate **class-conditionals** for a Bayes classifier; generation is a bonus viewpoint.

### 5. Why EM works here

For mixture models the posterior $p(z\mid x)$ is available in closed form via Bayes — so the “optimal variational $q$” is computable. Same idea extends to other latent-variable models when that posterior is tractable (HMMs mentioned as a historically notationally heavy example).

### 6. Bridge to MAP

MLE uses only data. With little data, MLE can be wild (e.g. five heads $\Rightarrow\hat p=1$). Next lectures put a **prior** on $\theta$ (Bayesian / MAP).

---

## Worked mini-example (generative draw)

$M=2$, $\alpha=(0.7,0.3)$, $\mu_1=-1$, $\mu_2=2$, unit variances. Roll: with probability $0.7$ draw from $\mathcal{N}(-1,1)$, else from $\mathcal{N}(2,1)$. The marginal density of $X$ is the two-bump mixture.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| $\alpha_j$ are free reals | They are mixture **probabilities** — simplex constraints. |
| E-step updates $\mu_j$ | E-step only updates $q$; M-step updates $\theta$. |
| GMM $\neq$ sampler | Fitting + ancestral sampling **is** generation. |
